front: What are the three rules of the Kubernetes networking model?
back: 1) All Pods can communicate with all other Pods on all nodes; 2) agents on a node (kubelet, kube-proxy) can communicate with all Pods on that node; 3) no NAT — every Pod reaches every other Pod using the Pod's real IP address.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Kubernetes Network Model

front: What are the three networks in a Kubernetes cluster?
back: Node network (real data-center/cloud network, one IP per node); Pod network (one IP per Pod, usually from the Pod CIDR range); cluster network (ClusterIP services, from --service-cluster-ip-range).
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Cluster Network Topology

front: How do containers within the same Pod communicate?
back: They share one network namespace (a single IP and port range) and communicate over localhost on different ports.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Pod Networking Internals

front: What is the pause (infrastructure) container?
back: A special container that starts first in a Pod and sets up the Pod's network namespace. Because it owns the namespace, application containers can restart without the Pod losing its IP/network stack. It shares the Pod's lifecycle.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Pod Networking Internals

front: What is the CNI (Container Network Interface)?
back: A standard specification Kubernetes uses to implement Pod/container networking. The CNI plugin (Calico, Cilium, Flannel, etc.) sets up namespaces, interfaces, bridges/tunnels, and IP addressing. Plugins are usually deployed as Pods via a DaemonSet.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — CNI

front: What is an overlay network and why use one?
back: An overlay gives the appearance of a single flat network between nodes and uses tunnels/encapsulation to move Pod packets between nodes, providing independence from the underlying network infrastructure while satisfying the no-NAT networking model.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Pod Communication Patterns

front: Why are Services needed in Kubernetes?
back: Pods are ephemeral — their count and IPs change. A Service provides a persistent virtual IP and DNS name as a stable front end and load balances traffic across the backing Pods, automatically updating as Pods come and go.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Understanding Services

front: How does a Service determine which Pods back it?
back: Via labels and selectors. A controller watches Pods matching the selector; each match gets an endpoint (Pod IP + target port) added to the load-balancing list. Remove a Pod's matching label and it is dropped from the Service (but keeps running).
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Understanding Services

front: What is kube-proxy and how does it run?
back: kube-proxy implements Services on the network. It runs as a Pod via a DaemonSet (one per node), watches the API server for Services/endpoints, and programs the local dataplane. Default mode is iptables; alternatives are IPVS and the legacy userspace mode.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Service Networking Internals

front: Differentiate port, targetPort, and nodePort in a Service.
back: port = port the Service listens on (clients connect here); targetPort = port the container/app listens on inside the Pod; nodePort = port opened on every node's IP (NodePort/LoadBalancer only), default range 30000–32767.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Defining Deployments and Services

front: What is a ClusterIP service?
back: The default Service type. Exposes the Service on a cluster-internal virtual IP reachable only inside the cluster. It is the foundation the other service types build on. Use for internal-only services or services fronted by Ingress.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — ClusterIP Internals

front: What additional services does a NodePort service create?
back: A NodePort service also creates a ClusterIP service. External traffic to <node-IP>:<nodePort> is routed by kube-proxy to the ClusterIP service, then to a Pod endpoint (possibly across the Pod network to another node).
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — NodePort Internals

front: How does a LoadBalancer service work, and what does it create?
back: It asks the cloud provider to provision a cloud load balancer with a public IP. It also creates a NodePort and a ClusterIP. Cloud LB → NodePort on nodes → ClusterIP → Pods. EXTERNAL-IP shows <pending> until the cloud provisions it.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — LoadBalancer Internals

front: What is an ExternalName service?
back: A Service of type ExternalName maps an in-cluster name to an external DNS name by creating a CNAME record. It has no selector and does no proxying — it just enables service discovery for services outside the cluster.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Other Types of Services

front: What is a headless service?
back: A Service with clusterIP: None. With selectors, DNS returns all matching Pod IPs (A/AAAA records) instead of a single virtual IP, letting the client choose. Common with databases and StatefulSets.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Other Types of Services

front: What is a service without selectors used for?
back: It lets you map a Service to manually created EndpointSlice/Endpoints objects with any IP/port (inside or outside the cluster). Multiple endpoints are load balanced. Used to manually control traffic targets while keeping service discovery.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Other Types of Services

front: What are EndpointSlices?
back: The modern way Kubernetes tracks Service endpoints (kubectl get endpointslices). They split endpoints into smaller chunks for better scalability than the legacy single Endpoints object.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Service Networking Internals (Kubernetes docs)

front: Imperatively expose a deployment named hello-world as a NodePort on port 80 → container port 8080.
back: kubectl expose deployment hello-world --port=80 --target-port=8080 --type=NodePort
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Defining Deployments and Services

front: How do you list the endpoints backing a Service named hello-world and check Pod labels?
back: kubectl get endpoints hello-world (or kubectl get endpointslices); kubectl describe service hello-world; kubectl get pods --show-labels to confirm labels match the selector.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Demo: ClusterIP

front: What DNS server does Kubernetes use and how is it deployed?
back: CoreDNS. By default a Deployment runs 2 CoreDNS Pods in kube-system for load balancing/resilience, fronted by a ClusterIP service named kube-dns (default 10.96.0.10) on port 53 UDP/TCP.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Cluster DNS

front: What is the FQDN pattern for a Service in cluster DNS?
back: <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local — e.g. hello-world.default.svc.cluster.local. The 'svc' segment and 'cluster.local' cluster domain are constant. Services get A/AAAA records.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Cluster DNS Records

front: What is the DNS A-record pattern for a Pod?
back: <pod-ip-with-dashes>.<namespace>.pod.cluster.local — e.g. 192-168-206-124.default.pod.cluster.local.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Cluster DNS Records

front: Where is CoreDNS configured, and what is the config file called?
back: In a ConfigMap named coredns in the kube-system namespace, mounted into the Pod at /etc/coredns as a file named Corefile. Edit with: kubectl edit configmap coredns -n kube-system. Default forwarding is 'forward . /etc/resolv.conf'.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Custom DNS Forwarders

front: What is the default Pod dnsPolicy, and what does dnsPolicy: None require?
back: Default is ClusterFirst (cluster domain → cluster DNS, everything else → node DNS). dnsPolicy: None ignores cluster DNS and requires you to define dnsConfig (custom nameservers/searches). Note: the value 'Default' means inherit from the node, and is NOT the default.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Custom Pod DNS Configuration

front: Why prefer DNS over environment variables for service discovery?
back: Env vars are injected only for Services that exist at Pod startup; a Service created after the Pod won't appear in its env until the Pod is recreated. DNS is dynamic and updates without restarting Pods.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Service Discovery

front: Distinguish an Ingress resource, an Ingress controller, and an IngressClass.
back: Ingress resource = the rules (hosts, paths, TLS). Ingress controller = the implementation (a reverse proxy that reads the rules and routes traffic); must be deployed separately. IngressClass = links an Ingress resource to a specific controller via spec.ingressClassName.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Ingress Architecture

front: Why use Ingress instead of a LoadBalancer service?
back: Ingress works at Layer 7 (HTTP), enabling path-based routing, name-based virtual hosts, URL rewriting, and session persistence; one controller fronts many services on one IP. LoadBalancer services are Layer 4 and expose one service per IP/port. Use L4 LoadBalancers for non-HTTP TCP/UDP.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Why Use Ingress Rather Than Load Balancers

front: What do the Ingress pathType values Prefix, Exact, and ImplementationSpecific mean?
back: Prefix = partial prefix match (/red matches /red and /red/1). Exact = exact, case-sensitive match only. ImplementationSpecific = matching delegated to the IngressClass/controller.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Path-Based Routing

front: How do you create a TLS Secret for Ingress, and how is TLS terminated?
back: kubectl create secret tls tls-secret --key tls.key --cert tls.crt, then reference it under spec.tls.secretName. TLS terminates at the controller on port 443; traffic from the controller to the Pod is unencrypted on port 80.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — TLS with Ingress

front: Name the three core Gateway API resources and their roles.
back: GatewayClass (cluster-scoped, defines a controller-backed class — provider). Gateway (an instance with listeners: protocol/port/TLS — operator). HTTPRoute (protocol-specific routing rules attached to a Gateway via parentRefs — developer). API group: gateway.networking.k8s.io.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Ingress Architecture (Kubernetes docs)

front: How does the Gateway API differ from Ingress?
back: It separates roles (GatewayClass/Gateway/Route) instead of one resource, supports more protocols (HTTP, TCP, UDP, gRPC), provides portable expressive matching and traffic splitting in-spec (not via annotations), and supports cross-namespace routing with ReferenceGrant. Installed as CRDs.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Ingress Architecture (Kubernetes docs)

front: How does NetworkPolicy behave by default, and what does it require?
back: With no policy, all ingress/egress is allowed. Once any policy selects a Pod for a direction, that direction becomes default-deny and only allowed traffic passes. Policies are additive (union; no explicit deny). Enforcement requires a CNI that supports NetworkPolicy (Calico, Cilium, etc.).
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — CNI (Kubernetes docs)

front: Write a NetworkPolicy that denies all ingress and egress for every Pod in the default namespace.
back: apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1, kind: NetworkPolicy, metadata.name: default-deny-all, namespace: default; spec.podSelector: {} (selects all Pods); spec.policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress] with no ingress/egress rules.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — CNI (Kubernetes docs)
